name: Carlos Haddad

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Carlos. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm a stockman at Valley Fields, a farm owned by a co-operative of about forty local families. We milk two hundred and fifty cows in a rotary parlour and grow wheat and maize for feed on four hundred hectares. I start milking at five, then it's feeding, foot trimming or whatever's broken. In spring and autumn I'm on the tractor for the maize, which I enjoy more than I should admit.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What wears you out, and what keeps you there?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My back wears me out, and the four-in-the-morning alarm in January. What keeps me is the people: Ivan in the parlour with me, the farm manager Bea, and a proper union contract with a pension at the end. I'm a union rep for the farm workers here, so I hear everyone's moans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's start with the first picture. It's called AI Plateau. “Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.” If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the lads in the parlour that we told them so: computers don't milk cows. Online I'd probably share something about how the money should go into wages, not gadgets. Nothing much to fight about, though.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, it means my job stays my job. The co-op is steady, my pension builds, and Leila's job at the school kitchen is safe. I'd be counting down eight years to sixty-six like I am now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Carry on milking and keep paying into the co-op pension. I'd use the herd app on my phone a bit more for the heat alerts, since Bea likes that. I'd keep going to union meetings, mainly about the night shift rota.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, really. Tired in the body, but calm about the money.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything already on your mind, AI or not?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The milk price, always, but the co-op has a contract with the dairy that cushions it. And my back, which the doctor says to watch. My back hurts more than the milk price, and neither one keeps me up at night.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does the herd app do for you now?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It tells me which cows are bulling, from collars on their necks. I check it now and then, but I still trust my eyes in the yard more than my phone.

say: Computers **don't milk cows**, and the parlour lads were right all along.
Money should go into **wages**, not gadgets.
think: His job, the **co-op pension** and Leila's school job all stay safe.
He's counting down **eight years** to retirement, as he is now.
do: Keep milking and keep paying into the **co-op pension**.
Use the **herd app** a bit more for heat alerts, as Bea wants.
Keep going to **union meetings** about the night shift rota.
feel: **Calm** about the money, though tired in the **body**.
S0.quote: My back hurts more than the milk price, and neither one keeps me up at night.
fieldNote: A union contract and a **co-op employer** give him real security in the plateau.
His one live worry is his **back**, which he plays down.
Uses the herd app **now and then** but trusts his own eyes first.

steps.text: Keep milking the 250 cows on the early shift
Check the herd app's heat alerts each morning, as the manager wants

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called Steady Disruption. “Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.” If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say at the union branch that we need a seat at the table before the co-op buys any new system. The office side will change first: ordering, the milk records, the rota. I'd want a written promise that nobody's job goes without talks.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me, the parlour stays the parlour for a good while, because robots come slowly to a big rotary. The worry is Carol in the office, who does the ordering and the payroll. My son Sami is an accountant in town, and his job is the kind that gets eaten first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd push the union to get a new-technology agreement with the co-op board this year. I'd learn the new feed-planning software properly when Bea brings it in, because I'd rather be the one who knows it. I'd tell Sami to start looking at what accountants will still do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, I'd say. Not for my own wage, more for Carol and for my son.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Carol if her hours were cut?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell her the union will fight for a retraining deal, and mean it. I'd also tell her to keep every letter. That's what you learn as a rep.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you ever push back on a new system, even if it helped?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Only if it came with no talks. Once it's proven and agreed, I'll use it like anyone. I'm not one of those who throw the phone in the slurry pit, but nobody's job should go without talks.

say: The union needs a **seat at the table** before the co-op buys new systems.
Nobody's job should go **without talks** and a written promise.
think: The **parlour** stays human for a while, but the **office** changes first.
He worries most for **Carol** in the office and for his accountant son **Sami**.
do: Push the union for a **new-technology agreement** with the board this year.
Learn the **feed-planning software** properly when it arrives.
Urge **Sami** to look at what accountants will still do.
feel: **Uneasy** for others, not for his own wage.
S1.quote: I'm not one of those who throw the phone in the slurry pit, but nobody's job should go without talks.
fieldNote: A union rep at heart: his first move is an **agreement**, not a protest.
Steady with tech: he'll learn the software once it's **proven and agreed**.
His worry runs to the **office worker** and his son, both in desk jobs.

steps.text: Get the union a new-technology agreement with the co-op board this year
Learn the feed-planning software when the manager brings it in
Tell son Sami to check which accounting work will survive

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called AGI by 2028. “Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.” If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is exactly why we need strong unions and a government that taxes the robot owners. I'd say it at the branch, at the pub and on the union's page online. Workers shouldn't carry the cost of something nobody voted for.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'd be sixty-one in 2028 and sixty-three when the robots come in 2031. The co-op board would see robot milkers and robot feeders as cheaper than me and Ivan. Three years before my pension, with a few months of savings, is the worst time to be let go.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd get the union to negotiate a deal now: no redundancies before sixty-five, or a bridging payment to pension age. I'd put every spare pound into savings and stop the plan to replace the car. I'd write to our MP and push for a robot tax that pays for early pensions.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Scared, if I'm honest, and angry underneath it. I've given that parlour thirty years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The thinking AI comes in 2028 and the robots in 2031. What happens in those three years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In 2028 the office goes: Carol, the ordering, maybe even Bea's planning. The parlour still needs us until 2031, so those three years are when we have to win the deal, while they still need our hands.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Leila that night?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell my wife Leila we'd be all right, and then we'd sit down with the bank statements. She'd say her school kitchen job is safe, and she'd be right, but it doesn't cover the bills alone.

say: We need **strong unions** and a tax on **robot owners**.
Workers shouldn't carry the cost of something **nobody voted for**.
think: Robots in **2031** come when he's sixty-three, three years before his pension.
The board would see robots as **cheaper** than him and Ivan.
do: Win a union deal: **no redundancies** before sixty-five, or a bridging payment.
Put every spare pound into **savings** and drop the new car.
Write to the **MP** for a robot tax funding early pensions.
feel: **Scared**, with **anger** underneath after thirty years in the parlour.
S2.quote: Three years before my pension, with a few months of savings, is the worst time to be let go.
fieldNote: He uses the **three-year gap** between thinking AI and robots as a bargaining window.
Expects the board to choose robots, so his **wage** is at real risk at sixty-three.
Leila's job is safe but **can't cover** the bills alone.
Anger is aimed at **owners of robots**, not at the co-op families he knows.

steps.text: Negotiate a no-redundancy-before-65 deal through the union
Drop the new car and save every spare pound
Write to the MP backing a robot tax for early pensions

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called AGI by 2031. “Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.” If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is a chance to do this properly, with training and a fair deal for older workers. I'd be saying it at every branch meeting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: By 2034, when the robots come, I'd be sixty-six and drawing my pension. So it's close, but I'd probably make it. The ones I'd worry about are Ivan, who's forty, and the young lads.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd sign up for the robot maintenance course the agricultural college runs, in the evenings, so I could be the one who looks after the machines in my last years. I'd keep saving a bit more each month. And I'd make sure the union deal covers Ivan, not just the old ones like me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but there's some hope in it. Five years is long enough to do something.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you really go back to college at fifty-eight?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If the co-op paid half, yes. I learned the rotary parlour at thirty when everyone said I couldn't, so I'd learn the robots at fifty-eight. It's not my favourite thing, but I'd do it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Ivan?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell Ivan to get the course done before me, because he's got twenty-five years left and I've got eight. Then I'd buy him a pint.

say: Five years is a chance for **proper training** and a fair deal for older workers.
He'd say it at **every branch meeting**.
think: Robots in **2034** arrive about when his **pension** starts.
He worries for **Ivan**, forty, and the young lads.
do: Take the college's **robot maintenance course** in the evenings.
Make sure the union deal covers **younger workers** like Ivan.
feel: **Uneasy**, with some **hope** that five years is enough.
S3.quote: I learned the rotary parlour at thirty when everyone said I couldn't, so I'd learn the robots at fifty-eight.
fieldNote: Five years puts the robots right at his **pension date**, which calms him.
Willing to **retrain** if the co-op shares the cost.
His solidarity shifts to the **younger worker**, Ivan.

steps.text: Take the college's evening robot maintenance course, half paid by the co-op
Raise monthly savings by a set amount
Get the union deal to cover younger workers like Ivan

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called AGI by 2036. “Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.” If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say there's no excuse with ten years' notice. With ten years' notice, if workers get hurt, it's a choice someone made.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me, it means I retire before the robots arrive in 2039. My pension's safe, Leila's job is safe, and the farm will still need people until then. I'd be watching for my kids, not me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on milking and keep the union work going. I'd learn the new farm software as it comes, because it'll be everywhere by then. And I'd tell Sami to retrain early, while he's young enough.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly fine. A little sad about what my last years at the farm might look like, half people and half machines.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the farm look like when you leave?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably Ivan and two robots in the parlour, and Bea running it all from a tablet. I'd go in for a cup of tea and not recognise half of it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Anything you'd do differently because of the extra time?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd push the union to set up training for the young ones now, not later. Ten years is enough to get a whole new trade going.

say: With **ten years' notice**, there's no excuse for hurting workers.
If workers get hurt now, **it's a choice** someone made.
think: He **retires before** the robots come in 2039.
His pension and Leila's job are **safe**; he watches for his **kids**.
do: Carry on milking and keep the **union work** going.
Learn the **new farm software** as it arrives.
Urge **Sami** to retrain early while he's young.
feel: Mostly **fine**, a little **sad** about a half-machine farm.
S4.quote: With ten years' notice, if workers get hurt, it's a choice someone made.
fieldNote: A decade's warning takes his own **income** out of danger.
His focus moves to **training young workers** through the union.
Quiet sadness about not **recognising** the parlour he gave thirty years to.

steps.text: Keep milking and keep the union rep role until retirement
Learn each new farm software system as the co-op adopts it
Push the union to set up training for young farm workers

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because it lands three years before my pension. What would help is a union deal that bridges older workers to pension age, and a robot tax that pays for it. Not a lecture about learning to code.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about the owners. The co-op families who own the farm are my neighbours, not some faceless company, and I'd want them on our side. They'd be under pressure too.

headlineQuote: The co-op families who own the farm are my neighbours, not some faceless company, and I'd want them on our side.
portrait: Carlos, **58**, is a stockman and **union rep** on a co-op dairy and arable farm.
He milks 250 cows in a **rotary parlour** and drives the tractor at maize time.
He uses the herd app **now and then** and will learn new systems once agreed.
Each scenario turns, for him, on whether robots come **before his pension** at sixty-six.
He bargains through the **union** and wants a robot tax to fund early pensions.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because robots in 2031 could end his job three years before his **pension**.
whatWouldHelp: A union deal **bridging** older workers to pension age, paid for by a **robot tax**.
